Vaginally administered cocaine overdose in a pregnant woman. Obstet Gynecol 1989; 74: 476–7. 2. Peretti FJ, et al. Cocaine fatality: an unexplained blood concen- tration in a fatal overdose. Forensic Sci Int 1990; 48: 135–8. 3. Karch SB, et al. Relating cocaine blood concentrations to toxic- ity–an autopsy study of 99 cases. J Forensic Sci 1998; 43: 41–5. PREGNANCY. The effects of cocaine abuse during pregnancy have been reviewed.1-4 Women who abuse cocaine during pregnancy appear to have an increased risk of spontaneous abortion,5 abruptio placentae6,7 and associated still-births,8 premature labour,9-11 and other birth complications.9-11 These effects may be due to vasoconstriction by cocaine increasing maternal blood pressure and reducing placental blood flow.12 Uterine rupture13 during pregnancy and rupture of ectopic pregnancies14 have also been associated with cocaine. Neo- nates born to mothers abusing cocaine have an increased risk of intra-uterine growth retardation and may have lower birth- weight, smaller head size, and shorter length.6,8-10,15-17 Co- caine is possibly teratogenic and congenital abnormalities as- sociated with abuse include cardiovascular abnormali- ties,9,18,19 limb reduction defects,20 intestinal atresia or infarction,20 skull defects,8 and genito-urinary tract anoma- lies.21 Neurobehavioural impairment22 and signs of transient CNS irritability23 may also occur. Some workers24,25 have found effects on cognition and motor delays while others have found effects on arousal and attention regulation rather than cognitive processes.26 Cocaine can increase neonatal cerebral blood flow27 and cerebral infarction and associated seizures have occurred in neonates whose mothers took co- caine near to the onset of labour.28 Evidence on the risk of intraventricular haemorrhage is conflicting.7,24 1.
